MOBILE-001.prerequisites: The target application's APK (Android) or IPA (iOS) file, obtained from the app store or provided by the client. Standard mobile reverse-engineering tools: apktool/jadx for Android, and a jailbroken test device or a static-analysis tool (class-dump, otool) for iOS. A rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator to run the app with debugging attached.
MOBILE-001.whatItIs: The version of the app published to real users still has debug settings turned on — things like Android's 'debuggable' flag left true, verbose logging that shouldn't be there, or hidden test menus reachable through a secret tap pattern. Any of these expose functionality or information that was never meant for regular users.
MOBILE-001.rootCause: Debug settings are genuinely useful during development — attaching a debugger, verbose logs for troubleshooting, test menus for QA. But they need to be explicitly turned off before the app ships. That step either got missed in the release process, or nothing automatically checks for it, so a debug-enabled build made it all the way to the app store.
MOBILE-001.impact: A debuggable production build allows any user (or attacker with physical/USB access to a device running the app) to attach a debugger and inspect or modify the app's runtime behavior, bypassing client-side security checks (license validation, root detection, certificate pinning) trivially; verbose logging can leak sensitive data to the device log; and hidden test menus can expose functionality (an admin panel, an unthrottled API test harness) never meant to be reachable by end users.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the APK and check the AndroidManifest.xml for `android:debuggable="true"` on the application element, which should never be present in a release build.
For iOS, inspect the app's entitlements (via `codesign -d --entitlements`) for `get-task-allow` set to true, which indicates a debug-signed build rather than a proper distribution/App Store build.

Attempt to attach a debugger (jdb for Android, lldb for iOS on a jailbroken device) to a running instance of the installed app and confirm whether the attach succeeds without any anti-debug countermeasure.
Search decompiled code/strings for test-menu trigger patterns, hidden Intent actions, or verbose logging statements that shouldn't be present in a production build.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse engineering and debugger-attachment testing against the test installation.
Confirm the debuggable flag/entitlement is present via manifest/entitlement inspection.
Attach a debugger to the running app and set a breakpoint on a security-relevant function (a license or root-detection check) to confirm unhindered runtime inspection/modification is possible.
If a hidden test menu or debug-only functionality is found, trigger it and document exactly what it exposes.
Document the specific debug artifact (manifest flag, entitlement, hidden menu) and its practical exploitability via debugger attachment.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

mitigation: Ensure `android:debuggable` is explicitly set to `false` (or omitted, which defaults to false) in the release build variant, and verify this via an automated build-pipeline check rather than manual review alone.
Sign iOS release builds with a proper App Store/Ad Hoc distribution profile that does not include `get-task-allow`, and verify entitlements as a release-gate check.
Strip all test menus, verbose logging, and debug-only code paths from release builds via build-flavor separation (a distinct debug source set never merged into release).
Add automated static analysis (MobSF or an equivalent) to the CI/CD pipeline to catch debug-flag and entitlement misconfigurations before a build reaches the app store.

MOBILE-002.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator. A decompiler (jadx for Android, class-dump/Hopper for iOS) to inspect WebView configuration and any JavaScript-bridge interface code. A proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to intercept and modify content loaded into the WebView.
MOBILE-002.whatItIs: The app uses a WebView (an embedded browser) to show web content, but sets it up insecurely — turning on JavaScript along with a bridge that lets loaded web content call sensitive native app functions, allowing it to load any file on the device, or loading content over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS. If an attacker can control what content gets loaded (by intercepting traffic, compromising an ad network, or a malicious link), they can run code with access to whatever that native bridge exposes.
MOBILE-002.rootCause: A WebView is powerful and general-purpose, and setting it up securely means getting several easy-to-miss settings right — limiting the JavaScript bridge to fully trusted sources, blocking universal file access, forcing HTTPS-only content. When a bridge gets added for a legitimate reason (letting web content call native app code) without also locking down which content is allowed to use it, anything the WebView loads — including something an attacker controls — inherits that bridge's power.
MOBILE-002.impact: An attacker who can get the WebView to load attacker-controlled or attacker-modified content (via a MITM position on an insecurely-loaded page, a malicious redirect, or exploiting a separate injection point elsewhere in the app that ultimately loads into the WebView) can invoke the exposed native JavaScript-bridge methods directly, potentially reading local files, accessing device sensors/contacts, or executing arbitrary native functionality depending on what the bridge exposes.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate all WebView instantiations, checking their configuration for `setJavaScriptEnabled(true)` combined with `addJavascriptInterface()` (Android) or an equivalent `WKScriptMessageHandler`/`window.webkit.messageHandlers` bridge (iOS).
For each JavaScript bridge found, review what native methods/classes it exposes and assess whether any allow file access, sensitive data retrieval, or arbitrary code execution.

Check whether the WebView restricts content loading to a specific, trusted origin (via `shouldOverrideUrlLoading`/`WKNavigationDelegate` origin checks) or loads any URL it's given, including ones reachable via a deep link or a MITM-redirected request.

Test whether the WebView has universal file-access enabled (`setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs`/`setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs` on Android) which would allow a loaded local HTML file to read other local files via `file://` URLs.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes MITM/content-injection testing against the test installation's WebView.
Identify a WebView loading content over an insecurely-verified channel (HTTP, or HTTPS without certificate pinning) and position a proxy to intercept and modify that content.
Inject JavaScript into the intercepted page content that invokes the exposed native bridge method(s) identified during discovery.
Confirm the injected JavaScript successfully triggers the native functionality (e.g. retrieves a piece of device data, reads a local file) as proof of concept.
Document the exact bridge method(s) exploited, the content-loading weakness that allowed injection, and the resulting native-functionality access achieved.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Universal file-access enabled, allowing a loaded local or attacker-supplied HTML file to read arbitrary local files via `file://` URLs independent of any JavaScript-bridge exposure.

Disable universal file access and universal access from file URLs unless there is a specific, well-understood need, and never combine either with an exposed JavaScript bridge.
Expose only the minimal set of native methods genuinely required through the bridge, and validate/sanitize all parameters passed from JavaScript before acting on them natively.
Where feasible, avoid WebView-based hybrid architectures for security-sensitive functionality entirely, preferring native UI for anything touching sensitive data or device capabilities.

MOBILE-003.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator with Frida available for runtime instrumentation. A decompiler to locate the biometric-authentication call site and understand how its result is checked.
MOBILE-003.whatItIs: The app uses fingerprint or face unlock to protect something sensitive (opening the app, approving a payment), but it decides whether that worked just by checking a simple true/false result in its own code, instead of using the successful unlock to release an actual cryptographic key that only a genuine, real authentication could unlock. That true/false check can be forced to 'true' using standard runtime tampering tools, completely bypassing the biometric check without ever actually scanning a real fingerprint or face.
MOBILE-003.rootCause: The phone's biometric system itself is genuinely tamper-resistant at the hardware level. But if the app only uses it as a simple yes/no flag in its own logic ('unlock succeeded, so set this flag to true and continue'), instead of tying that unlock to actually releasing a protected key from secure hardware, the real security boundary is just an ordinary function call inside the app — something that can be intercepted and manipulated.
MOBILE-003.impact: An attacker with local code execution or debugger/instrumentation access to the device (a jailbroken/rooted device, or malware with sufficient privilege) can force the authentication-success callback to fire regardless of whether real biometric verification occurred, completely bypassing the intended authentication gate and accessing whatever sensitive functionality it was meant to protect — a fake fingerprint is not even needed since the biometric prompt itself can be skipped entirely by hooking the result callback.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the app and locate the biometric-authentication call site, checking whether the success callback merely sets a boolean flag consumed elsewhere in application logic, or is used to unwrap/decrypt a cryptographic key tied to the Keystore/Secure Enclave.
Attach Frida to a running instance and enumerate the class/method implementing the biometric callback interface to confirm it's hookable.
With authorization, hook the identified success-callback method to force it to report success, then attempt to proceed past the biometric prompt without providing genuine biometric input.

Where the app does bind to a Keystore/Secure Enclave key, separately verify that the key's access policy genuinely requires biometric authentication for use (`setUserAuthenticationRequired` correctly configured) rather than being retrievable through some other, unguarded code path.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime instrumentation of the test installation's biometric-authentication flow.
Attach Frida to the running app and hook the biometric-authentication success-callback method identified during discovery.
Trigger the app's biometric prompt, then use the hook to force a success result regardless of what (if anything) is presented to the actual biometric sensor.
Confirm the app proceeds to the protected functionality despite no genuine biometric verification having occurred.
Document the exact hooked method, the bypass technique, and whether the underlying sensitive operation (a Keystore-protected key) was also actually bypassed, or only the app's own boolean gate.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-004.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device, with a test account. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to capture and replay session tokens, and the ability to control device/network state to simulate a lost/stolen-device or extended-idle scenario.
MOBILE-004.whatItIs: The app's login session stays valid forever, or for an unreasonably long time, with no expiration, no timeout after inactivity, and no real way to revoke it. Once issued, the same session keeps working for every future request, no matter how much time has passed, whether the user logged out on another device, or whether the phone itself was reported lost or stolen.
MOBILE-004.rootCause: Session length and revocation were built around convenience — not making users log in repeatedly — without the server actually enforcing a maximum lifetime, an inactivity timeout, or a real revocation check on every request. The token's validity depends only on whether it was ever issued, not on whether the session is actually still legitimate right now.
MOBILE-004.impact: A token captured via any means (device theft, a MITM interception, a backup extraction) remains usable by an attacker indefinitely, or at least for far longer than a properly-bounded session would allow, and a user who explicitly logs out on one device (believing this to end their session) may find the same token still valid and usable from a captured copy, undermining their own expectation of having terminated access.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a valid session token during normal app use via a proxy, then attempt to reuse it after progressively longer periods of app inactivity to determine whether any idle-timeout enforcement exists server-side.

Perform an explicit "log out" action within the app, then attempt to replay the previously-captured token directly against the backend API (bypassing the app UI) to check whether the server actually invalidates it, or whether logout is purely a client-side state change.
Check whether the token has a JWT-style expiration claim (`exp`) and, if so, whether the server actually enforces it or merely issues it as informational metadata the client happens to respect.

Determine whether any "log out of all devices"/session-management feature exists in the app, and if so, confirm it actually invalidates previously-issued tokens server-side rather than only affecting the current session's local state.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes session-token capture and replay testing against the test installation using a test account.
Capture a valid session token via the proxy during normal app use.
Perform an explicit logout within the app, then replay the captured token directly against the backend API and confirm whether it's still accepted.
If accepted, wait a representative extended period (or simulate device-loss conditions) and replay again to further characterize the token's effective, unbounded lifetime.
Document the exact token type, its claimed vs. actual expiration behavior, and whether logout provides genuine server-side revocation.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Validate token expiration server-side on every request rather than trusting the client to respect a claimed expiration value.

MOBILE-005.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device with Frida available. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with its CA certificate available, and a certificate-pinning-bypass script set (objection's built-in bypass, or a curated public bypass-script collection) appropriate to the app's pinning implementation.
MOBILE-005.whatItIs: The app does implement certificate pinning (checking that it's really talking to the real server), but the way it's built has a weakness that lets standard, publicly available bypass tools defeat it anyway — maybe it's only enforced in some parts of the app but not others, or the check itself is a simple, easy-to-intercept comparison, or the app uses a popular library's pinning feature in a way that public bypass scripts already specifically target.
MOBILE-005.rootCause: Pinning was added, but without extra protection making it resistant to runtime tampering tools (like Frida) — no obfuscation of the check itself, no anti-hooking measures, no redundant checks. A pinning check that's technically present but easily bypassed gives a false sense of security if it's never actually tested against the tools that would defeat it.
MOBILE-005.impact: An attacker who can hook and neutralize the pin-validation function achieves the same full MITM interception capability as if certificate pinning were entirely absent (see the related missing-certificate-pinning finding for the resulting impact), meaning the practical security benefit of having implemented pinning at all is effectively negated for any attacker who is aware of and can run standard, off-the-shelf bypass tooling against a rooted/jailbroken device.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the app does implement some form of certificate pinning (via decompilation, looking for a pin-comparison or a well-known pinning library's initialization) as distinct from the missing-pinning finding.

Attach Frida with a standard, publicly-available universal SSL-pinning-bypass script (objection's `android sslpinning disable`, or an equivalent iOS script) and attempt to intercept the app's HTTPS traffic through a proxy while the bypass is active.
If the standard bypass succeeds without modification, this confirms the pinning implementation is defeatable by widely-available tooling rather than requiring bespoke reverse engineering.

Check whether pinning is enforced consistently across every network call the app makes, or only on some endpoints (a common partial-implementation gap even when the core pinning mechanism itself is reasonably robust).
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime instrumentation and MITM proxy testing against the test installation's pinned network traffic.
Set up the intercepting proxy with its CA certificate installed on the test device's trust store.
Attach Frida with the appropriate universal SSL-pinning-bypass script for the platform and networking library in use.
Attempt a normal, sensitive network action (login, an API call) within the app and confirm the proxy successfully captures the decrypted traffic despite the app's pinning implementation being active.
Document which specific bypass script/technique succeeded and note any endpoints where pinning enforcement appeared inconsistent.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

variants: Pinning implemented via a third-party networking library (OkHttp CertificatePinner, TrustKit) with a known, publicly-documented bypass technique specific to that library's implementation pattern.

Implement multiple, independent pinning checks at different layers (network library level and an additional application-level check) so defeating one doesn't automatically defeat the other.

Periodically re-test pinning robustness against current, publicly-available bypass tooling as part of routine mobile security assessments, since bypass techniques and tooling evolve.

MOBILE-006.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device connected to a network you control. A packet-capture tool (Wireshark/tcpdump) or a transparent network proxy positioned to observe all of the app's network traffic, independent of whether the app attempts certificate pinning (since this finding covers traffic sent without TLS at all, not a pinning bypass).
MOBILE-006.whatItIs: The app sends data over plain, unencrypted HTTP for at least one of its network features — maybe the main API is fine, but an analytics service, an update check, or a third-party ad SDK sends data unencrypted — instead of using HTTPS for absolutely everything the app talks to over the network.
MOBILE-006.rootCause: Not every part of the app that talks over the network got the same 'always use HTTPS' treatment. This usually happens because a secondary feature — analytics, ads, an update check — was added by a different team or a third-party SDK, and it never went through the same security review that covered the main API traffic.
MOBILE-006.impact: Any network-path observer (a malicious/compromised Wi-Fi access point, an on-path attacker via ARP spoofing on a shared network) can passively capture and read the unencrypted traffic, and where it carries authentication credentials, session tokens, or sensitive user data, achieve credential theft or session hijacking; where the channel also lacks any integrity protection, active tampering (injecting malicious content into an update-check response, for example) is possible too.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the app's full network traffic during a comprehensive walkthrough of every feature (login, primary functionality, settings, and any background/update-check activity) using Wireshark or a transparent proxy configured to capture all traffic, not just HTTP(S).

Filter the capture for any traffic on standard unencrypted ports/protocols (HTTP on port 80, or a custom unencrypted protocol) rather than assuming all traffic is HTTPS based on the app's primary, most visible functionality.
For each unencrypted channel found, identify what data it carries and flag any credential, token, or sensitive user data specifically.

Check the app's manifest/configuration for Android Network Security Config or iOS App Transport Security (ATS) settings, since an overly permissive exception (`cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"` or an ATS exception domain) is frequently the specific configuration enabling this finding.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes network traffic capture during a full feature walkthrough of the test installation.
Capture traffic across every feature of the app, including background/secondary channels not immediately visible in the primary UI flow.
Identify and extract any sensitive data observed in cleartext.
Where credentials/tokens are captured, attempt to use them against the corresponding service as proof-of-impact evidence, using only test accounts.
Document every unencrypted channel found, the data it exposed, and the specific Network Security Config/ATS configuration responsible for permitting it.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-007.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for decompilation. A decompiler (jadx for Android, Hopper/class-dump for iOS) to locate random-value-generation call sites, and a scripting environment to statistically test generated output for predictability if source access allows extraction of the generation routine.
MOBILE-007.whatItIs: The app generates a value that needs to be genuinely unpredictable — a session token, a password-reset code, an encryption value — using an ordinary random-number function (like Math.random()) instead of one specifically designed to be cryptographically secure. Or it uses the right kind of secure generator, but starts it off with a predictable seed (like the current time), which narrows down how unpredictable the output really is.
MOBILE-007.rootCause: Regular random functions are simpler to use and perfectly fine for things like animations or test data — but they're not built to resist someone trying to guess the output. It's easy to overlook the difference between 'random enough for everyday use' and 'genuinely unpredictable enough to be secure' when a developer just grabs the first random function that comes to mind instead of deliberately picking the secure one for something sensitive.
MOBILE-007.impact: Where the predictable value is used for something security-critical (a password-reset token, a session identifier, a cryptographic nonce/IV), an attacker who can characterize the generator's algorithm and seed (often straightforward for well-known non-cryptographic PRNGs, whose internal state can be fully reconstructed from a small number of observed outputs) can predict future or past values, potentially forging valid tokens, hijacking sessions, or breaking the confidentiality guarantee of an encryption scheme relying on nonce/IV uniqueness and unpredictability.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for random-value generation call sites, flagging any use of `java.util.Random`, `Math.random()`, or C's `rand()`/`srand()` in a context that produces a security-sensitive value (tokens, IVs, nonces).

For each flagged call site, trace how the generated value is seeded — an explicit, predictable seed (current time, a device ID) is a more severe variant even if the underlying algorithm were otherwise acceptable.

Where the app communicates with a backend, capture multiple instances of the security-sensitive value (e.g. successive password-reset tokens for test accounts) and statistically analyze them for a discernible, non-random pattern.

Confirm whether a proper CSPRNG (`SecureRandom`, `SecRandomCopyBytes`) is available and used elsewhere in the same app for other purposes, indicating the specific flagged use is an inconsistency rather than a codebase-wide gap.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse-engineering and predictability-testing of the identified random-value generation routine.
Extract or replicate the exact non-cryptographic generation algorithm and seeding logic identified via decompilation.
Collect a representative sample of generated values (e.g. successive test-account password-reset tokens) via authorized test requests.

Attempt to reconstruct the generator's internal state from the collected sample and predict a subsequent value, then confirm the prediction is accepted as valid by the backend (e.g. successfully using a predicted reset token).
Document the exact generation routine, seeding weakness, and the demonstrated predictability/forgery achieved.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

Audit the codebase for all random-value generation call sites as part of a security-focused code review, distinguishing security-sensitive uses (requiring a CSPRNG) from general-purpose ones (where a standard PRNG remains acceptable).

Where server-side generation is feasible for a given value (e.g. password-reset tokens), prefer generating it server-side using the server platform's CSPRNG rather than relying on client-side generation at all.

MOBILE-008.prerequisites: At least two separate installations of the target application (on two different test devices, or two separate app-data resets on the same device) for comparison. A decompiler to locate the key-generation/retrieval logic, and a means to extract the actual key material from each installation for comparison.
MOBILE-008.whatItIs: The app uses the exact same encryption key on every single device it's installed on, either because that key is hardcoded directly into the app, or because the code that generates it always produces the same result regardless of the device — instead of generating and securely storing a unique key for each individual installation.
MOBILE-008.rootCause: Generating a genuinely unique key per device and storing it securely takes deliberate extra work — using the phone's secure key storage to create and hold a key tied specifically to that device. Just embedding one shared key directly in the app is much simpler, but it means anyone who extracts that key from any single copy of the app (which requires no special access to any particular victim's phone) gets a key that works for every other installation too.
MOBILE-008.impact: Any attacker who extracts the shared key from any single copy of the app (which they can freely download and reverse-engineer themselves, requiring no access to any specific victim's device) obtains a key that decrypts data protected by that same key on every other user's device, turning what should be a per-user or per-device compromise into a universal, all-users compromise from a single extraction effort.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the cryptographic key-generation or key-retrieval logic used for locally-encrypted data.

Determine whether the key is a literal, hardcoded value in the binary, or is generated/derived using any per-installation or per-device-specific input (a securely-generated random value stored in platform secure storage, or a value derived from device-specific hardware identifiers).
Install the app on two separate devices (or reset and reinstall on the same device) and extract the key material from each installation using the identified generation/retrieval logic.
Compare the extracted key values directly — identical values across independent installations confirm the shared-key finding.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes key extraction and comparison across multiple test installations.
Extract the key material from a first test installation using the method identified via decompilation.
Extract the key material from a second, independent test installation using the same method.
Confirm the two extracted keys are identical, proving the key is shared rather than uniquely generated per installation.
Demonstrate impact by using the extracted key from one installation to decrypt locally-protected data from the other installation, confirming cross-installation decryption succeeds.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-009.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with its CA certificate installed into the device's trust store, and a means to route the app's traffic through the proxy (system proxy settings, or a VPN-based traffic-capture app).
MOBILE-009.whatItIs: The app talks to its server over HTTPS but does no certificate pinning at all — it just relies entirely on the phone's built-in list of trusted certificate authorities. That means any certificate the phone trusts (which anyone can get for a domain they own, or one added by installing a rogue certificate) is enough for someone to sit in the middle of that 'secure' connection.
MOBILE-009.rootCause: Certificate pinning was never added, probably because it adds ongoing work — coordinating pin updates whenever the certificate gets renewed, and handling pin failures gracefully so a routine cert renewal doesn't break the app for everyone. That extra effort got deprioritized in favor of just shipping without it.
MOBILE-009.impact: An attacker positioned on the network path (a malicious/rogue Wi-Fi access point, a compromised local network, or a device with a maliciously-installed rogue CA certificate) can transparently intercept and modify all traffic between the app and its backend — including login credentials, session tokens, and any sensitive business data in transit — without the app raising any warning to the user.
stepsToIdentify: Install the testing proxy's CA certificate into the test device's trust store (a straightforward, unprivileged action on most test devices/emulators) and configure the app's traffic to route through the proxy.
Launch the app and exercise any network-dependent feature (login, data sync, an API call) while observing whether the proxy successfully decrypts the traffic.
If traffic is fully visible in the proxy without any connection failure or app-level warning, certificate pinning is confirmed absent.
Cross-reference against the certificate-pinning-bypass-specific finding to distinguish this (no pinning at all) from a case where pinning is present but defeatable.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

Install the proxy's CA certificate into the test device's trust store and route the app's traffic through the intercepting proxy.
Perform a normal, sensitive action within the app (login, an API call involving test data) and confirm the proxy captures the decrypted content.
Document the specific sensitive data observed in the intercepted traffic as impact evidence.

Note whether the interception succeeded with no special effort beyond standard proxy/CA setup, distinguishing this finding's low-effort exploitability from a scenario requiring an active pinning bypass.

MOBILE-010.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device (or an emulator with root access) sufficient to access the app's private data directory directly. File-system search/inspection tools, and a decompiler if the storage appears encoded rather than cleartext.
MOBILE-010.whatItIs: The app stores sensitive data — cached credentials, session tokens, personal user info, business data — in plain, readable form inside its own private storage area (like a local database or settings file), instead of encrypting it with a properly managed, device-secured key.
MOBILE-010.rootCause: This private storage area was treated as automatically safe, on the assumption that the phone's normal app sandboxing (which does stop other apps from reading it) is protection enough. That doesn't account for a rooted or jailbroken phone, a full device backup being extracted, or someone physically accessing a lost or stolen phone — all of which get around that sandbox entirely and expose whatever is stored there in plain text.
MOBILE-010.impact: Anyone with root/jailbreak access to the device, access to an unencrypted device backup, or physical access combined with forensic extraction tools can directly read the sensitive data without needing to compromise the app's own authentication or authorization layer at all — turning a single device-level compromise into full data exposure regardless of how well the app's own network-facing security controls are implemented.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application normally to generate representative sensitive data (log in, perform typical actions) then access the device's private app-data directory directly (via root/jailbreak access, or `adb shell run-as` for a debuggable Android app).
Inspect SharedPreferences/UserDefaults XML/plist files, local SQLite databases, and any flat files in the app's private directory for plaintext sensitive content.
For content that appears encoded rather than cleartext, attempt straightforward decoding (Base64, simple XOR) before concluding genuine encryption is in use.

Check whether the platform's proper secure-storage facility (Android Keystore-backed EncryptedSharedPreferences, iOS Keychain) is used for genuinely sensitive fields specifically, or whether everything is stored in ordinary, unencrypted app-private storage.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

Access the app's private data directory using root/jailbreak access (or `adb shell run-as <package>` for a debuggable build) and extract the relevant storage files.
Confirm the data is readable in plaintext (or trivially decodable) without needing the app's own credentials or any additional secret.
Document the exact storage location, the type of sensitive data found, and the storage format (plaintext, weakly encoded, or genuinely but improperly encrypted).
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-011.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with access to external/shared storage (an SD card, or Android's shared external storage partition). Standard file-system browsing (via `adb shell` or a file-manager app) — no root/jailbreak required, since external storage is, by definition, more broadly readable than the app's private sandbox.
MOBILE-011.whatItIs: The app saves sensitive cached files — downloaded documents, cached data containing personal info, temporary exports — to shared external storage on the device (historically readable by any app with basic storage permission), instead of its own private, sandboxed storage area.
MOBILE-011.rootCause: External storage is sometimes used just because it has more free space, or because one specific feature genuinely needs to place a file somewhere another app can reach it, like sharing a document. But that same external location often ends up reused for other, more sensitive files that were never meant to be reachable by other apps, without anyone going back to separate the two use cases.
MOBILE-011.impact: Any other app installed on the device with storage-read permission (a broadly-granted, commonly-requested permission on older Android versions especially) can read the sensitive cache files without needing any special privilege or user interaction beyond having been granted ordinary storage access, exposing cached PII, documents, or API response data to any malicious or overly-permissioned app sharing the device.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application normally to trigger caching behavior (viewing a document, browsing content that gets cached) and monitor what files get written to external/shared storage locations.

Inspect the written files' content for sensitive data (PII, cached API responses, document content) rather than assuming external-storage writes are always for genuinely shareable/non-sensitive content.
From a separate, unprivileged test app (or a plain file-manager app) with only ordinary storage-read permission, attempt to read the same files to confirm cross-app accessibility.

Check the app's target SDK version and storage-access-framework usage, since scoped storage (introduced in more recent Android versions) narrows but doesn't always fully eliminate this exposure depending on how the app requests and uses storage access.

MOBILE-012.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. Access to the app's assetlinks.json (Android App Links) or apple-app-site-association (iOS Universal Links) file, hosted on the associated domain, and the ability to construct and send a crafted deep link to the test device.
MOBILE-012.whatItIs: The app registers to automatically open specific website links directly (instead of in a browser), but this is only supposed to work once the linked website proves — through a small verification file it hosts — that it actually authorizes this specific app to do so. If that verification is missing or misconfigured, or if the app also accepts the same links through an older, unverified method, any other unrelated app can register for those same links and intercept them instead.
MOBILE-012.rootCause: This link-verification setup depends on a correctly formatted file being hosted at a specific location on the website in question, and any mistake there — a missing file, a wrong ID, wrong file headers — makes the phone quietly fall back to treating it as an ordinary, unverified link that any app claiming to handle it can grab. This can go unnoticed during development because the app might still open correctly on the developer's own test device due to a cached verification result.
MOBILE-012.impact: A malicious app installed on the same device can register itself as a handler for the same link pattern and intercept links intended for the legitimate app — including, in security-sensitive flows, an OAuth redirect URI or a password-reset link — potentially capturing an authorization code, a reset token, or other sensitive data carried in the link's parameters before the legitimate app ever sees it.
stepsToIdentify: Fetch the domain's `assetlinks.json` (Android) or `apple-app-site-association` (iOS) file directly and verify it's present, correctly formatted, and lists the correct package name/bundle ID and signing-certificate fingerprint for the legitimate app.

Check whether the app also registers a custom URL scheme (`myapp://`) as a fallback or alternative to the verified App Link/Universal Link, since custom schemes have no equivalent domain-ownership verification and can always be claimed by any other app.

Install a benign test app on the same device that registers an intent-filter/URL-scheme matching the target's link pattern, and send a test deep link to confirm which app's chooser (if any) appears, or whether the test app intercepts it silently.

Review what sensitive data (OAuth codes, reset tokens, session identifiers) is carried as parameters in the app's deep links, since exploitability severity depends heavily on what's actually exposed if interception succeeds.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes installing a test interceptor app on the same device as the target app and sending crafted deep links.
Verify the association-file configuration issue via direct HTTP fetch, or confirm the app falls back to an unverified custom URL scheme.
Install a benign test app registering the same link pattern/custom scheme as the target app.

Send a deep link carrying a representative sensitive parameter (a test OAuth-style authorization code or reset token) and confirm whether the test interceptor app receives it instead of, or in addition to, the legitimate app.
Document the specific association-file misconfiguration (or custom-scheme fallback) and the sensitive parameter type confirmed interceptable.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-013.prerequisites: The target application's APK for decompilation. A device or emulator with adb access to send Intents directly to exported components, bypassing the app's own UI entirely.
MOBILE-013.whatItIs: A piece of the Android app (a screen, a background service, a way of receiving system messages) is marked as available to other apps on the device, without also requiring any special permission to use it — meaning any other installed app can directly trigger that piece of functionality, completely skipping whatever access checks the app's normal screens and navigation would enforce first.
MOBILE-013.rootCause: Making a component available to other apps is often genuinely necessary — for example, to handle a 'share' action from another app. But that availability was set more broadly than needed, or wasn't paired with a permission requirement limiting which other apps can actually use it. The setting alone doesn't distinguish between 'any app should be able to call this' and 'any app technically can, but really shouldn't.'
MOBILE-013.impact: A malicious app installed on the same device can directly invoke the exported component with attacker-controlled Intent extras, bypassing any access control or input validation the app's normal UI-driven flow would have applied before reaching that code path — depending on what the component does, this can range from triggering unintended functionality to a full authentication bypass (if the exported component is, for example, a post-login Activity reachable without ever passing through the actual login screen) or arbitrary file read/write (if it's a ContentProvider exposing more than intended).

Use `adb` to directly invoke each flagged component with crafted Intent extras, bypassing the app's normal UI navigation entirely, and observe the resulting behavior.

Prioritize findings where the exported component reaches security-sensitive functionality (a post-authentication screen, a data-export ContentProvider, a privileged BroadcastReceiver) over one exposing genuinely benign, intentionally-shareable functionality.

Confirm the component processes the crafted Intent and executes the sensitive functionality as proof of concept (e.g. reaching a post-login screen without authenticating, or reading data via an overly permissive ContentProvider).

Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-014.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA. String-extraction and decompilation tools (strings, jadx for Android, class-dump/Hopper for iOS), and, if secrets appear encoded, a scripted approach to test common encodings against extracted candidates.
MOBILE-014.whatItIs: The app itself contains hardcoded secrets — third-party API keys, backend passwords, encryption keys, cloud credentials — built directly into the compiled app or its resource files, instead of being fetched securely at runtime after the app proves who it is to a backend server.
MOBILE-014.rootCause: Developers typed these credentials directly into the app's code or resource files during development, often just to make integrating a third-party service easier — and that practice carried straight through into the version that got published. Since a mobile app is, by nature, distributed to and fully controllable by every single user who downloads it, anything embedded in it becomes effectively public the moment it's published — there's no such thing as a 'private' secret buried inside a public app.
MOBILE-014.impact: Extraction of any hardcoded credential grants the attacker whatever access that credential provides — a third-party API key can be abused for unauthorized usage billed to the organization's account, a backend service credential can grant direct database or infrastructure access, and a cloud-provider key can expose broader cloud-account resources — often extending well beyond the individual app instance being tested, since the same hardcoded secret typically applies to every installed copy of the app.

MOBILE-015.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A means to send crafted input to the app's various input surfaces: Intent extras (Android), file-open/import handlers, and inter-app data-sharing endpoints (a shared ContentProvider, a Share-sheet target).
MOBILE-015.whatItIs: The app accepts input coming from another app or a shared file (something opened via a 'share' or 'open with' action) without properly checking its structure or content first — which, depending on how that unchecked input gets used, can cause anything from a crash to unauthorized file access or unexpected behavior in another part of the app.
MOBILE-015.rootCause: Input checking usually gets built for the app's own normal screens, but not consistently applied to input arriving from other apps or shared files. This reflects an assumption that this kind of input would only ever come from trustworthy, well-behaved sources — not a potentially malicious app or a deliberately crafted file.
MOBILE-015.impact: Depending on where the unvalidated input flows, impact ranges from application instability/crashes (a low-severity denial of service triggerable by any other app on the device) to path traversal (reading/writing files outside the intended directory via a maliciously-crafted file-import path) or logic errors that a malicious co-located app could exploit to manipulate the target app's behavior without any user interaction.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every IPC/file-import input surface: exported components accepting Intent extras, share-sheet targets, and any custom file-format the app opens/imports.

For each surface, craft and send malformed or boundary-testing input (oversized strings, unexpected data types, path-traversal sequences, null bytes) via adb or a benign test app, observing for crashes or unexpected behavior.

Trace how each input flows through the app (does it become a file path, is it parsed by a file-format handler, does it reach a WebView or a database query) to understand what specific vulnerability class a validation gap enables.

Cross-reference findings against more specific, related test cases (the exported-component and WebView findings) since a general input-validation gap is often the root enabler for those more specific issues.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed-input testing against the test installation's IPC/file-import surfaces.
For each surface, systematically supply boundary/malformed values via adb or a benign test app and observe application behavior.
Where a path-traversal-shaped input is accepted via a file-import feature, attempt to read/write a file outside the app's intended working directory as proof of concept.
Where the unvalidated input flows into a WebView or another downstream component, escalate testing toward the specific relevant finding rather than treating this as a standalone terminal finding.
Document each vulnerable input surface, the specific malformed value that triggered unexpected behavior, and the resulting impact observed.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-016.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for permission-manifest review. A test device to install the app and observe actual permission usage during normal operation, correlating requested permissions against features genuinely exercised.
MOBILE-016.whatItIs: The app asks for phone permissions — location, contacts, camera, microphone, storage, SMS — that go beyond what its actual features actually need. Maybe a permission is left over from a feature that got removed, was requested speculatively for something that never shipped, or is set to a broader level (like background location) than the feature genuinely requires.
MOBILE-016.rootCause: Permission requests often get copied from a default SDK setup, requested ahead of time for features that were planned but never built, or just never revisited as the app's actual functionality changed over time. Since asking for an extra permission has no immediate visible downside to the developer beyond a slightly longer consent screen for the user, there's little natural pressure to trim the list down to only what's actually used.
MOBILE-016.impact: Excessive permissions increase the app's potential impact if it's ever compromised (via a separate vulnerability, a malicious update, or a supply-chain-compromised third-party SDK bundled within it) since the compromised code inherits whatever the app's granted permissions allow — a data-exfiltration payload embedded in a compromised app with background-location and contacts access has far more to steal than one confined to only the permissions its legitimate functionality actually needs.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and list every permission declared in the manifest (Android) or Info.plist usage-description entries (iOS).

Map each declared permission against the app's actual, observable features (through normal use and, where necessary, code review of what each permission-gated API is used for) to identify permissions with no corresponding feature.
Pay particular attention to broad or sensitive permissions (background location, SMS read, contacts) and confirm via code review that they're genuinely exercised, not just requested defensively.

Check whether any bundled third-party SDK is the source of an otherwise-unexplained permission request, distinguishing a first-party over-request from a third-party dependency's own broad requirements.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through manifest/permission review and code-usage correlation rather than actively exploited by the tester, since "exploitation" here is really a demonstration of the excess-privilege risk rather than a direct technical attack.
Confirm scope authorizes reviewing the test installation's permission declarations and correlating them against actual feature usage.

Where feasible, demonstrate the risk concretely by identifying a separate finding elsewhere in the app (an injection point, an insecure IPC surface) that could be chained with the excessive permission to illustrate realistic amplified impact — e.g. a compromised WebView bridge that could, given the app's granted background-location permission, exfiltrate ongoing location data.
Document each permission found to lack a corresponding, currently-active feature, distinguishing first-party requests from third-party-SDK-driven ones.

Recommend the client adopt a documented permission-justification process for each release, where every requested permission (first-party or SDK-introduced) is explicitly mapped to a shipping feature before the build is published.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-017.prerequisites: The target application's push-notification handling code (via decompilation) and, where testing black-box, the ability to send a crafted push notification to a test device — either via an authorized backend test endpoint, or a compromised/spoofed push-sending credential if that's a separate, related finding in scope.
MOBILE-017.whatItIs: The app's push notification handler acts on the content of a notification — like opening a specific screen, or triggering a data update — without properly checking that it actually came from a trustworthy source or matches the format it expects.
MOBILE-017.rootCause: Push notifications are usually treated as automatically trustworthy, since they're normally only sent by the app's own legitimate backend. But if the credential used to send pushes is ever compromised, or if the app doesn't independently double-check the content of what it receives, anyone able to send a push to the app can trigger unintended behavior through it.
MOBILE-017.impact: A malicious or spoofed push payload can trigger unintended app behavior without any user interaction beyond receiving the notification — executing an embedded deep link that navigates to a sensitive screen, triggering a client-side action based on an untrusted data field, or, in the most severe case, exploiting a separate parsing vulnerability in how the payload's data is processed, achieving impact ranging from unwanted navigation/UI disruption to a more serious client-side vulnerability chain.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the push-notification receiver code, tracing how it processes the payload's data fields — particularly any that trigger navigation, deep-link execution, or a client-side action.
Check whether the receiver validates the payload's structure/content against an expected schema, or trusts and acts on any field present without validation.
With authorization and access to a test-sending mechanism, send a crafted payload with an unexpected or malformed data field and observe the app's behavior.
Assess whether the push-sending credential/backend configuration has any additional protection (e.g. payload signing) that an app-side validation gap might otherwise be masked by.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending crafted push-notification payloads to the test installation via an authorized test-sending mechanism.
Craft a payload with a data field designed to trigger unintended app behavior (an unexpected deep-link target, a malformed action instruction) based on the receiver logic identified during discovery.
Send the crafted payload to the test device and observe whether the app processes it as designed by the attacker.

Where a more serious downstream vulnerability is reachable via the payload (a WebView load, an exported-component-style action), escalate testing toward that specific finding rather than treating this as standalone.
Document the exact receiver logic gap and the resulting unintended behavior achieved.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-018.prerequisites: The target application's update-check code (via decompilation). A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) capable of modifying the update-check response, and, where certificate pinning is also present, an authorized bypass technique from the related pinning findings to intercept this specific traffic.
MOBILE-018.whatItIs: The app has its own custom system for checking whether an update is available (separate from the app store's built-in one), and it asks a server for the latest version and download link — but doesn't properly verify that response is genuine. It just trusts whatever version number and URL it gets back, with no cryptographic check. That lets an attacker who intercepts or fakes that response redirect the app to install something malicious, or falsely claim there's no update when there actually is a critical one.
MOBILE-018.rootCause: The update-check response is trusted simply because it's assumed to arrive over a secure connection, without any additional signature or authenticity check on top of that. If that connection is ever compromised (especially if certificate pinning is weak or missing, as covered in a related finding), or if the update server itself is compromised, there's nothing else standing in the way of a tampered response being trusted.
MOBILE-018.impact: An attacker able to intercept or spoof the update-check response can redirect users to a malicious, attacker-hosted "update" (chaining into the related insecure-in-app-update-bypassing-official-store finding for full impact), or can suppress a legitimate critical security update by always reporting the current version as up-to-date, leaving users unknowingly running a vulnerable version indefinitely.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the custom update-check logic, confirming it exists as a distinct mechanism from relying solely on the official app store.

Trace how the update-check response (version number, download URL) is processed — is any cryptographic signature verified over the response content, or is it trusted based on transport security alone.

With authorization, intercept the update-check response via a proxy (using an authorized certificate-pinning bypass if pinning is present) and modify the version number/download URL, observing whether the app accepts the tampered response.
Test both directions: forcing acceptance of a malicious "update" and forcing suppression of an available update by always returning the current version as latest.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes update-check response interception and modification testing against the test installation.
Intercept the app's update-check request via the proxy and prepare a modified response with an alternate version number and/or download URL.
Replay the modified response to the app and confirm whether it's accepted without any signature/authenticity verification.

Where accepted, demonstrate the resulting impact — either the app proceeding to download from the attacker-specified URL, or the app failing to prompt for an update the tampered response falsely claims is unnecessary.
Document the exact update-check mechanism, the missing authenticity verification, and the demonstrated tampering impact.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-019.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device supporting biometric authentication. Ability to disable/fail biometric authentication (or simply decline it) to trigger the fallback flow, and standard PIN-brute-force testing patience (or automation via adb/Frida) if the fallback lacks rate limiting.
MOBILE-019.whatItIs: The app uses fingerprint or face unlock as its main way to protect access, but the backup option — used when biometrics fail or aren't available — is a short PIN (usually just 4 digits) with no limit on how many times someone can guess wrong. That makes the backup path far weaker than the biometric one it's supposed to match in strength.
MOBILE-019.rootCause: A short PIN backup is added for convenience — people expect a quick, simple fallback when biometrics don't work — without giving it the same security treatment as the primary biometric method. Specifically, there's no limit on repeated wrong guesses, which is exactly the protection a short, easy-to-guess PIN absolutely needs to be acceptably secure.
MOBILE-019.impact: An attacker with physical access to an unlocked-but-idle device (or a device where biometric auth can be conveniently declined to fall through to the PIN prompt) can brute-force a 4-digit PIN in a bounded, often quite short amount of time (a maximum of 10,000 combinations, frequently far fewer given common PIN-selection patterns) if no lockout mechanism throttles repeated attempts, gaining full access to whatever the biometric gate was meant to protect.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the app's fallback authentication flow (decline or fail biometric authentication) and confirm the fallback mechanism's exact form (PIN length, alphanumeric vs. numeric-only).
Attempt a sequence of incorrect PIN entries and observe whether any rate-limiting, increasing delay, or lockout threshold is enforced after a defined number of failures.

If no lockout is observed within a reasonable number of manual attempts, assess the full keyspace size and calculate the maximum time required for an automated brute-force (via adb input injection or Frida) to guarantee success.
Confirm whether the PIN fallback protects the same sensitive functionality as the biometric primary path, or only a lesser subset, to correctly scope the impact.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes PIN brute-force testing against the test installation's fallback authentication mechanism.
Trigger the fallback PIN prompt.

Using adb input injection (or Frida to directly call the PIN-verification function) automate submission of the full PIN keyspace (or a representative common-PIN dictionary first, for efficiency) without manual re-entry for each attempt.
Confirm whether any lockout engages during the automated attempt sequence, and if not, continue until the correct PIN is found or the full keyspace is exhausted.
Document the exact keyspace size, lockout behavior (or its absence), and the time required to guarantee successful brute-force.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-020.whatItIs: A home-screen widget shows sensitive information directly — account balances, recent messages, personal details — including in situations where that widget is visible on the lock screen before the phone is even unlocked, exposing that data to anyone who can just glance at the screen.
MOBILE-020.rootCause: Widgets exist to show useful info at a glance without opening the full app, and the convenience of doing that was prioritized without considering that widgets can be visible on the lock screen — a place where the same information would normally require unlocking the phone and opening the app to see.
MOBILE-020.impact: Anyone with physical proximity to the device — a bystander, someone who has stolen or found the device, or a person glancing at it in a public setting — can view sensitive information directly from the lock screen without any authentication challenge, undermining the app's own in-app authentication controls entirely for whatever data the widget chooses to surface.

MOBILE-021.prerequisites: The target application's update mechanism (if it implements a custom, non-store-based update flow). A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to intercept and modify the update-package download, and a benign proof-of-concept APK/IPA to substitute in place of the legitimate update.
MOBILE-021.whatItIs: The app has its own system for downloading and installing updates outside of the official app store — common for internal/enterprise apps — and that custom update system doesn't properly check that the downloaded file is genuine and untampered (a real signature check against the vendor's known key) before installing it. On Android, this sometimes means requesting permission to install packages directly and installing them with no signature check at all.
MOBILE-021.rootCause: Skipping the official app store's update system also means giving up the free, built-in signature verification the store normally provides. If the custom update system doesn't rebuild an equivalent check on its own, the downloaded update is trusted just because it came from the expected web address over a (hopefully) secure connection — a much weaker guarantee than a real cryptographic signature check.
MOBILE-021.impact: An attacker able to intercept or redirect the update-download channel (a network MITM position, or a compromise of the distribution server itself) can deliver an arbitrary, attacker-controlled APK/IPA that the user is prompted to install believing it to be a legitimate update — resulting in full compromise of the user's device with whatever permissions the substituted malicious app requests, since it appears to originate from the trusted vendor's own update process.

Decompile the app to trace the update-download and installation code path, checking whether any cryptographic signature verification occurs against the downloaded package before the install prompt is triggered.

With authorization, intercept the update-download traffic via a proxy and substitute a different, clearly-labeled benign test package, observing whether the app proceeds to prompt for its installation.

Check whether the app checks the downloaded package's certificate/signature against a pinned, expected value (not just checking that a signature exists at all, which any self-signed package would trivially satisfy).

Intercept the download via the proxy and substitute a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept package in place of the legitimate update.
Observe whether the app proceeds to the installation prompt for the substituted package without any signature-mismatch warning.
Document the exact verification gap (no check, or a check that doesn't validate against the vendor's actual expected signing key) and the resulting installation-prompt behavior.

MOBILE-022.prerequisites: The target application and a second, benign test app installed on the same test device, both authored/controlled by the tester if inter-app data sharing needs to be simulated. Standard IPC-inspection tooling (adb, Frida) to observe shared data.
MOBILE-022.whatItIs: The app shares data with other apps on the phone — through a shared storage mechanism, a shared file, or a broadcast message — in a way that exposes more data, or exposes it to more apps, than the specific feature it's meant for actually requires.
MOBILE-022.rootCause: This kind of sharing is usually built to support one specific, legitimate need — like sharing a document with another app, or syncing with a companion app from the same company. But the sharing mechanism ends up configured more broadly than that one use case needs, often because narrowing it down (to just that one verified companion app, for example) takes more deliberate setup than a general-purpose, open sharing method.
MOBILE-022.impact: Any other app on the device (not just the intended companion/integration partner) can access the shared data, which may include more sensitive fields than the sharing feature's user-facing purpose would suggest — turning a narrow, intended integration into a broad exposure to any app a user happens to have installed, including a malicious one.

MOBILE-023.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device with Frida available. A decompiler to locate Keychain/Keystore API usage and its configured access-control attributes.
MOBILE-023.whatItIs: The app stores something sensitive (a login token, an encryption key) in the phone's secure credential storage — but sets it up too loosely, like not requiring the phone to actually be unlocked to retrieve it, or not requiring a fingerprint/passcode check when accessing it. So even though the secure storage system is being used, its actual protection is much weaker than it could be.
MOBILE-023.rootCause: Just using the phone's secure storage system is often treated as good enough by itself, without the extra step of configuring exactly how protected each stored item should be. The default settings for these systems often don't require an unlock or biometric check unless the developer specifically asks for that — so simply calling the secure-storage function without extra configuration gives a much weaker guarantee than the phone is actually capable of providing.
MOBILE-023.impact: Depending on the specific access-control gap, an attacker with a jailbroken/rooted device, or one who extracts a backup/device image, may be able to retrieve the stored secret without needing to unlock the device or pass biometric authentication at all — reducing the practical protection to little more than what an ordinary (non-secure-store) storage location would have provided, despite the app nominally following the "use Keychain/Keystore" best practice.

For iOS, check whether the Keychain item's accessibility constant is a restrictive one (`kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` or stricter, ideally paired with a biometric access-control flag) versus a looser default.

For Android, check whether the Keystore key was generated with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` and an appropriate validity duration, or whether it's usable without any authentication check at retrieval time.

With authorization on a rooted/jailbroken device, attempt to retrieve the stored item directly (via Frida hooking the retrieval call, or direct Keychain/Keystore inspection tooling) without providing device unlock/biometric confirmation, to confirm the gap is practically exploitable and not just a theoretical configuration concern.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes Keychain/Keystore item extraction testing on a rooted/jailbroken test device.
Identify the specific stored item and its configured access-control attributes via decompilation.
Attempt retrieval of the stored item using Frida or direct secure-storage inspection tooling, without providing device unlock/biometric confirmation.
Confirm whether retrieval succeeds despite the absence of the expected authentication step.
Document the exact item, its configured (insufficient) access-control attribute, and the successful bypass achieved.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

MOBILE-024.prerequisites: The target application's manifest/Info.plist for custom URL-scheme registration review. A means to send a crafted URL to the test device (adb, or a link within a test web page/another app) targeting the registered scheme.
MOBILE-024.whatItIs: The app registers its own custom link format (like 'myapp://') to handle certain actions, but the code that processes an incoming link doesn't properly check where that link actually came from before acting on it — accepting sensitive actions like logging in or changing a setting purely because a link said to, with no confirmation the link genuinely came from a trusted source rather than any random app or webpage.
MOBILE-024.rootCause: Custom link formats like this have no built-in way to prove which website or app is actually allowed to send them — unlike the newer, verified link system covered in a related finding. Any app on the phone, or any webpage in any browser, can build and trigger one of these links with whatever parameters it wants. If the app's handler trusts those parameters to perform something sensitive without double-checking where they came from, that link format becomes an open door anyone can knock on.
MOBILE-024.impact: Any malicious app or web page can trigger the same sensitive action the custom URL scheme exposes — silently logging a user into an attacker-controlled account (if the scheme is used for an OAuth-style callback without adequate state/origin validation), triggering an unwanted in-app action, or, in the most severe cases, executing a state-changing operation (a settings change, initiating a transaction) purely by getting the victim to click a link or load a malicious web page, entirely without the victim's informed consent to that specific action.
stepsToIdentify: Review the app's manifest/Info.plist for every registered custom URL scheme and decompile the corresponding handler code to understand what actions each URL path/parameter combination triggers.

Identify any handler that performs a sensitive, state-changing action (not just navigation to a screen) directly from URL parameters without an additional confirmation step or origin/source validation.

Craft a test URL replicating the sensitive action's parameter structure and trigger it via adb, a test web page, or a benign test app, observing whether the action executes without any additional user confirmation or source check.
Where the scheme is used for an OAuth-style redirect/callback, check specifically for state-parameter validation to rule out authorization-code interception/injection via this channel.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

Construct a test URL replicating that action's expected parameters.

Document the exact URL scheme, path/parameters, and the sensitive action achieved without proper authorization.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member
